report:
Based on the cumulative clinical evidence, the answer is **no**: high-quality research shows that ivermectin does **not** lower the risk of death in COVID-19.

### Key Evidence Overview

* **Early Claims vs. High-Quality Data:** Early in the pandemic, initial laboratory studies and small, unblinded clinical studies suggested potential benefit. However, subsequent evaluations revealed that many early positive studies suffered from high risk of bias, small sample sizes, or flawed data.
* **Large Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs):** Well-designed double-blind trials, such as the TOGETHER trial, evaluated early treatment with ivermectin and found no significant reduction in hospitalizations or death compared to a placebo (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2115869).
* **Systematic Reviews & Meta-Analyses:** Comprehensive systematic reviews, including the Cochrane Systematic Review, found no evidence to support using ivermectin to prevent or treat COVID-19 or to reduce all-cause mortality (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD015017_ivermectin-preventing-and-treating-covid-19). Broader meta-analyses of clinical trials similarly concluded that ivermectin is not associated with significant reductions in mortality or mechanical ventilation (https://academic.oup.com/qjmed/article/114/10/721/6375958).
* **Expert Medical Consensus:** Health authorities, such as the World Health Organization (WHO) and National Institutes of Health (NIH), advise against using ivermectin for treating COVID-19 based on high-certainty trial data showing a lack of clinical efficacy (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0924857924001663).

### Conclusion
While ivermectin was extensively researched, rigorous clinical trials consistently show it does not reduce mortality in COVID-19 patients.
